1183-the-return-of-dr-fu-manchu:
Sax Rohmer brings back Dr. Fu Manchu, the "devil doctor" of Limehouse, for a second round against Nayland Smith of Scotland Yard and Dr. Petrie, his narrator. The villain's plots run through poison, secret societies, and Eastern intrigue, while Smith chases him across London.

Rohmer writes the pulp at full throttle, with cliffhangers, disguises, and exotic menace. The book, like its predecessor, trades on the fears of its age about the East. Read as a period thriller, it still grips, and it fixed Fu Manchu in popular myth. The chase still grips readers who enjoy pulp villains at full throttle.
173-the-insidious-dr-fu-manchu:
Dr. Petrie's quiet London night breaks when Nayland Smith bursts in with a warning. Sax Rohmer's Insidious Dr. Fu-Manchu introduces the criminal mastermind who seeks to restore Chinese power in the West. Smith, just back from Burma, hunts Fu-Manchu's agents through fog and secret rooms.

Poison, hypnotism, and exotic assassins fill the chase, told by the loyal Petrie. Fu-Manchu himself appears rarely, which makes him more fearsome. The novel's yellow-peril framing now reads as dated and prejudiced, a fact modern readers should weigh. It launched one of pulp fiction's most copied villains.
22241-the-ghost-in-the-white-house-some-:
Gerald Stanley Lee published The Ghost in the White House in 1920, as America chose a new president. Lee, a popular writer on crowds and genius, offers suggestions for a President whom everyone can work with. He presents a programme and a sketch of what the next President will be like as a fellow human being. Name, eyes, and party he leaves for others to fill in later.

The ghost of the title is the public's own imagined President, haunting the real one. Lee asks how a whole people can express what they want and actually get it. His style is breezy, paradoxical, and hopeful. The book is a period piece of post-war idealism about democracy.
43505-a-century-of-christian-service-ken:
C Silvester Horne, minister of Kensington Chapel, wrote a centenary history of Kensington Congregational Church, covering 1793 to 1893, with fourteen illustrations. Horne was the church's own minister and its historian. Chapter one treats the forming of the church. Portraits and chapel views fill the plate list.

Successive ministries structure the narrative: the first ministry, then Rev John Clayton's brief one. Sixteen years of progress under Rev John Leifchild follow, then prosperity under Dr Vaughan. Dr Stoughton's term enlarges the borders, and Dr Raleigh's is called gracious. A new church is planted under Rev C B Symes. Horne's own ministry chapter is titled To Be Continued.
45620-the-lost-and-hostile-gospels-an-es:
The Reverend S Baring-Gould wrote The Lost and Hostile Gospels, published in London and Edinburgh in 1874. Baring-Gould was known for books on religious belief and on the lives of Old Testament figures. His essay studies the Toledoth Jeschu, a Jewish counter-telling of the life of Jesus. It also studies lost gospels of which only fragments remain.

The first part asks why the historian Josephus stayed silent and what the Talmud says. The second part treats Petrine writings, such as the Gospel of the Hebrews and the Gospel of Peter. The third part covers Pauline-side texts, including gospels of Truth, Eve, Philip, and Judas. Baring-Gould writes for readers curious about the shadow side of early Christian literature.
53809-saint-john-chrysostom-his-life-and:
Saint John Chrysostom: His Life and Times is a biography by Stephens, printed at London by John Murray in 1880. The subtitle calls it a sketch of the church and the empire in the fourth century. Stephens was a prebendary of Chichester and rector of Woolbeding. He had already written the life and letters of Walter Farquhar Hook, and a book on Christianity and Islam.

The preface to the second edition explains the book's making. The edition is substantially a reproduction of the first. Stephens had revised the text and references and made slight alterations, but saw no defects grave enough to warrant rewriting the whole. Nine years of further study stand behind the small changes. The book is both a saint's life and a history of the late Roman church.
57603-a-daughter-of-jehu:
A Daughter of Jehu is a novel by Laura E Richards, who also wrote Abigail Adams and Her Times. It came out in 1918, with pictures. A joke in the front matter says she driveth furiously, like Jehu of old.

The story opens with Cyrus, then brings in Kitty, the heroine of the tale. Ross House and the Home Guard set the scene of a small town. Neighbours, a party and a skeleton in a cupboard stir the plot. The tone stays brisk and warm. Richards mixes humour with home truths about pride, haste and love. A song sheet, The Duke of Lee, is printed in the front matter.
58026-the-trial-and-conviction-of-that-i:
The Trial and Conviction of John Church is a pamphlet on a famous scandal, here in John Fairburn's edition of 1817. Church was the Surrey Tabernacle preacher in the Borough Road. He was tried at the Surrey assizes at Croydon on August 16, 1817, before Lord Ellenborough.

The charge is named on the title page as an abominable offence. The whole of the evidence, taken in shorthand, fills the pamphlet. His life, confessions, a sermon, and his love letters are added at the back. A rival edition is attacked in a puff on the cover. Readers get the raw print war over a preacher's fall, effigy burning and all.
68283-the-call-of-cthulhu:
The Call of Cthulhu is a horror story by Lovecraft, first published in the magazine Weird Tales in February 1928. An epigraph from Algernon Blackwood opens the tale. The narrative is framed as papers left by the late Francis Wayland Thurston of Boston.

The first part is called The Horror in Clay. The narrator begins with a mercy. The human mind, he says, cannot connect all it knows, and men live on a placid island of ignorance amid black seas of infinity. One day the piecing together of separate knowledge will open terrifying views of reality. The story then builds its case from a sculptor's bas-relief and old cult records. The hosted text comes from Project Gutenberg.
930-the-cook-s-decameron-a-study-in-tast:
Mrs. W. G. Waters wrote this study in taste, The Cook's Decameron, with more than two hundred recipes for Italian dishes. She quotes Talleyrand on dinner as a pleasure that comes every day and lasts an hour, and her preface recalls Montaigne on eating well. The book is dedicated to A. V., in memory of certain Ausonian feasts.

Waters treats Italian cooking as an art, not a chore, with recipes for soups, pastas, meats, and sweets, and notes on taste and season. Her prose is learned and appetising, for cooks who love Italy. The volume remains a charming early guide to Italian food in English, full of flavour and good sense.
britannica-1911-abbahu: 'Abbahu is the headword of a very short entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica. The entry names a Palestinian amora, a teacher of rabbinic tradition, who flourished from about 279 to 320. He urged Jews to study Greek, the entry states, a notable stance in his setting. He won fame as a collector of traditional lore. The Talmud cites him very often, the entry adds. Name, dates, one policy, and one habit of learning fill the whole notice in the opening volume of the 1911 edition.
britannica-1911-buchu:
Buchu, or buka leaves, come from shrubs of the genus Barosma. The plants grow at the Cape of Good Hope. This 1911 Britannica article describes the drug and its uses. The chief species is Barosma crenulata. Its leaves are smooth, leathery and oblong. They run an inch to an inch and a half long. Oil glands dot their edges and undersides.

Two other species also yield buchu leaves. Their leaves differ in shape and edging. All share a pale yellow-green colour in trade. They give off a strong aromatic smell. The taste is bitter and slightly astringent. The leaves hold a volatile oil. That oil yields a camphor-like deposit in air. Doctors once used buchu for urinary complaints. The British Pharmacopoeia lists an infusion and a tincture. The entry notes that newer synthetic drugs had made the remedy nearly obsolete.
britannica-1911-catechu:
Catechu is a trade article from the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a plant extract used in medicine and dyeing. It is also called cutch, from a Malay word. The main source is the wood of two kinds of acacia that grow in India, and that yield is known as black catechu. A paler kind, sold as gambir, comes from the leaves of a plant of the East Indian islands.

A third kind comes from the betel palm fruit. The article sets out how black catechu reached the market in three forms. The best, Pegu catechu, came in blocks wrapped in large leaves. A less pure kind came in masses moulded in sand. The third came as large cubes packed in coarse bags. The piece then turns to how the acacia wood is cut and worked once the trees have grown thick enough.
britannica-1911-jehu:
Jehu is a Bible article in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica about a general who became king of Israel. Jehu, son of Jehoshaphat and grandson of Nimshi, served Ahab and Jehoram. While Jehoram lay wounded at Jezreel after the war against Damascus, the prophet Elisha sent a messenger to anoint Jehu king. The general took the call, drove furiously to Jezreel, and killed both kings.

The article shows how later writers judged the coup. Israel's historians saw the coup as a religious revolution: the overthrow of Baal worship. The article describes the destruction of the prophets of Baal at Samaria, and Jehu's backing from the Rechabites. Yet the prophet Hosea denounced the bloodshed at Jezreel.
britannica-1911-sadhu:
Sadhu is the name for a Hindu ascetic, and this 1911 Britannica entry describes these holy men and their range of lives. They match the Muslim fakir and are also known as Sanyasis, Gosains, and Bairagis. They belong to many sects, hold odd views, and follow strange practices. Many put themselves through cruel hardships and fantastic disciplines as a path to holiness.

In standing they range from the wandering philosopher to the idle vagabond. Some live a life of quiet thought, which Hindus hold most holy. Others set up as alchemists, doctors, fortune-tellers, palmists, or acrobats. Some practise open tortures, holding an arm upright until it withers or lying always on a bed of spikes. Most wear a garment dyed orange-red with ochre, the source, the entry says, of the Mahratta flag's colour. Alone among Hindus, their dead are buried, not burned.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-coelchu:
James MacCaffrey's entry tells of Coelchu, also called Colga or Colcu. He was a learned abbot of the Irish school of Clonmacnoise in the later eighth century. A student of that school himself, he gave special study to Saint Paul. Paul became his patron saint. Coelchu earned the surnames Scribe and Wise for his learning. None of his own writings survive, though one devotional tract of his was still known in the seventeenth century.

Most of the entry turns on a letter Alcuin sent to Coelchu. It reports on religion on the Continent and names Joseph, a pupil of Coelchu then in France. It also mentions quarrels between King Charles and Offa of Mercia. Gifts of money from Charles and from Alcuin went to Clonmacnoise and to Irish monks. Those gifts date the letter to shortly before 790. The entry also weighs whether Alcuin had ever studied under Coelchu.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-jehu:
Jehu is the name of two Old Testament figures this entry treats in turn. The first, a prophet and son of Hanani, spoke against King Baasha of Israel, later rebuked King Jehoshaphat of Judah for allying with Ahab. He outlived him, and wrote the history of his reign.

The second Jehu, tenth king of Israel, was an army commander under Joram whom Elisha's messenger anointed at Ramoth-Gilead to avenge the house of Ahab. Hailed king by fellow officers, he rode to Jezreel, overthrew Joram, and began a bloody reign that purged Baal worship while binding Israel to new and costly wars.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-dichu:
Dichu, son of an Ulster chieftain, earns his place as the first person Patrick converted in Ireland. This entry tells a story of sudden reversal. A pagan lord, he first opposed Patrick's landing at the Slaney estuary in 432. He even attacked the saint. Yet he was won over on the spot and gave Patrick the barn at Saul for a church. The Catholic Encyclopedia piece of 1913 makes Saul the first Irish foundation of the national apostle.

From a man of war, Dichu became a model of peace. Saul grew into a famous abbey where Patrick himself often rested. Patrick eventually died there. Two of Dichu's sons, held hostage by King Laoghaire, were freed at Patrick's prayer. The entry is short, but it anchors a turning point. One lord's conversion opened a kingdom to a new faith.
podcast-dannyjones--FQghS0GRhU:
Science writer Nadia Drake joins host Danny Jones for a long conversation that ranges well past her usual beat. Drake has covered space for major outlets. Here she fields questions about moon bases and odd features reported on Mars. She also takes up the uncontacted tribes of the Amazon, who still live apart from the modern world.

Jones steers the talk toward what officials might not be saying, and Drake answers as a working investigator would, weighing claims against evidence. The mix is the appeal: one guest moving from lunar plans to jungle peoples in a single sitting. Listeners should treat the wilder claims as the speakers' own, offered in a podcast built for speculation as much as for reporting.
podcast-joerogan--tUMqudtrHU:
Comedian Matt Rife joins Joe Rogan to tell of his ghost hunt in the Conjuring House in a segment from the show. The house is the Rhode Island farm tied to the Perron family case and the hit horror film. Rife is a young comic with a huge online crowd.

Rife tells what his night in the house felt like, from the cold rooms to the sounds he could not place. He shares why he bought rights in the place, as he tells it. Rogan asks if he is now a true believer. Listeners get a fun, spooky tale. The library holds the segment as an archive record.
podcast-joerogan-5DRQP2CiMHU:
Back in episode 371 of the Joe Rogan Experience, Rick Doblin made an early version of the case he is still making today. Doblin founded the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelic Studies to turn banned drugs into legal medicines. At this point, that goal was still distant.

He explains the first trial results for MDMA as a treatment for PTSD and why he thought regulators could be won over. Rogan, new to the subject then, asks basic questions that keep the talk clear. Heard now, the episode is a time capsule: the starting line of a campaign that later reached the edge of approval.
the-cook-s-decameron-a-study-in-taste-co:
Mrs. W. G. Waters calls her book The Cook's Decameron, a study in taste holding over two hundred recipes for Italian dishes. A line from Talleyrand at the front praises dinner as a pleasure that comes every day and lasts an hour. Waters dedicates the book to A. V., in memory of certain feasts in Italy.

Her preface opens with Montaigne, who praised the high skill Italian cooking had reached in his day. Montaigne describes a cook from Cardinal Caraffa's kitchen who spoke of sauces, salads, and the order of service with grave, learned care, as if handling a deep point of faith. Waters notes that Englishmen tend to grant fine cooking to the French alone, and she asks only for tolerance toward the Italian art, not for any loss of credit to French cookery.
the-insidious-dr-fu-manchu:
Sax Rohmer opens this thriller in Dr. Petrie's rooms. The hour is half past ten at night. A gentleman is announced as a late visitor. Nayland Smith bursts in, sun-baked and lean. Petrie had thought him in Burma. Smith grips his friend's hands hard. He then puts out the lamp without warning. He peers from the window into the road. Only then does he relight the lamp. He laughs at his own mystery.

He admits he has good cause for caution. He promises Petrie marketable material instead. Uncanny mystery could free a doctor from dull practice. Broken legs and influenza pay less well. Rohmer launches the Fu-Manchu stories on that midnight visit. A colonial official has come home from the East. Darkness is watched from a window. A doctor becomes witness and chronicler.
the-return-of-dr-fu-manchu:
Sax Rohmer brings back his villain through a midnight summons to narrator Petrie. The Reverend J. D. Eltham, a former fighting missionary in China, asks when Petrie last heard from Nayland Smith, then turns the talk to the accursed Chinaman of the Dulwich cellar case.

Eltham, mild in looks and clerical in voice, stuffs his pipe fiercely while insisting he has never stopped wondering about Fu-Manchu since the burnt-out cottage affair. Whisky, tobacco, and dread fill the opening scene. Series readers get the familiar pairing of domestic calm and imperial peril restored at once.
